source: Halawi, Zhang, Yueh-Han, Steinhardt (2024) Approaching Human-Level Forecasting with Language Models - system
finding: First retrieval-augmented LM forecaster near the human crowd. Pipeline: LM writes search queries, news API returns articles, LM rates relevance and summarises, reasoning model forecasts, then an ensemble of 6 forecasts.
numbers: Data: 5 platforms (3,762 questions total, 914 in test). Test Brier: system .179 (SE .003) vs crowd .149; accuracy 71.5% vs 77.0%. Best no-retrieval baseline LM (GPT-4-1106): .208. Random .25. 5 retrieval dates per question.
limits: Crowd still better overall. Hyperparameters tuned on validation then frozen for test.
agent_relevance: Retrieval plus ensembling closes about 0.03 Brier of a 0.06 gap to the crowd; the rest remains. Reference design for S3.

source: Halawi, Zhang, Yueh-Han, Steinhardt (2024) Approaching Human-Level Forecasting with Language Models - ablations
finding: Retrieval is worth about 0.02 Brier; fine-tuning about 0.007; the hand-tuned reasoning prompt alone gave a small gain.
numbers: Table 5 ablation: full .179; fine-tuned GPT-3.5 in place of GPT-4 .182; base GPT-4 only (no fine-tune) .186; base GPT-4 with no fine-tuning and no retrieval .206 (best plain baseline was .208). Fine-tuning set 13,253 samples.
quote: Without fine-tuning and no retrieval ... attains a Brier score of .206
limits: Row labels of the table are garbled in text extraction; the .186 and .206 values are stated in the prose.
agent_relevance: Retrieval is the largest controllable gain (.206 to about .186). Prompt search is minor. Spend budget on search before prompt polish.

source: Halawi, Zhang, Yueh-Han, Steinhardt (2024) Approaching Human-Level Forecasting with Language Models - ensembling
finding: Appendix E.1: ensembling six base forecasts helps only a little. Trimmed mean (halve weight of the forecast furthest from the median) won. Asking an LM to aggregate (universal self-consistency) did NOT beat no ensemble.
numbers: Validation Brier, 6 base reasonings: mean .1656, median .1651, geometric mean .1655, trimmed mean .1649, USC .1691, no ensemble (average of base Brier) .1676, human crowd .1600. Gain of trimmed mean over a single run about .0027.
limits: Differences among mean, median and trimmed are about .0007, inside noise. Validation only. Same-model-family samples, so errors are correlated.
agent_relevance: Averaging 6-8 runs gives a small real gain (about 0.003). Supports G5: code aggregates; an LM aggregator was worse than a plain average.

source: Halawi, Zhang, Yueh-Han, Steinhardt (2024) Approaching Human-Level Forecasting with Language Models - where retrieval helps
finding: The system beats the crowd only in conditions: crowd unsure, early retrieval dates, many relevant articles. Weak where the crowd is confident (system hedges toward .5).
numbers: Crowd prob .3-.7: validation ours .199 vs crowd .246; test .238 vs .240 (51% of forecasts). Early dates 1-3: .185 vs .161. At least 5 relevant articles: .175 vs .143 (Brier falls as article count rises). All three conditions: .240 vs .247 (22% of forecasts, 43% of questions). Confident-crowd questions: +7% accuracy but Brier worse by .04.
limits: Conditions chosen after seeing validation patterns. Calibration fixes (binning, isotonic) did not help; system naturally calibrated but under-confident.
agent_relevance: Gate on evidence quantity: with few relevant articles trust the prior. Do not push to extremes without strong evidence (hedging cost).

source: Halawi, Zhang, Yueh-Han, Steinhardt (2024) Approaching Human-Level Forecasting with Language Models - crowd adjustment
finding: Averaging system and crowd beats either alone. Best weight was 4x for the crowd.
numbers: Full test set: crowd .149, weighted system+crowd .146 (gain .003). Unweighted average in the selective subsets beats the crowd in every row, e.g. crowd-uncertain subset .237 vs .240.
limits: Needs a live crowd forecast; gain on the full set only about .003.
agent_relevance: Origin of the 'crowd adjustment gained nearly 0.01' idea: blending with an external prior gives a small gain. The agent has no crowd; its analogue is blending with a base rate.

source: Schoenegger, Tuminauskaite, Park, Bastos, Tetlock (2024) Wisdom of the Silicon Crowd - Study 1
finding: Median of 12 diverse LLMs (no retrieval) was statistically indistinguishable from 925 human forecasters on 31 Metaculus binary questions, and beat the 0.25 no-skill line.
numbers: LLM crowd Brier M=0.20 (SD .12) vs .25: t(30)=-2.35, p=.026 (BH-adjusted .039). Vs human crowd M=0.19 (SD .19): t(60)=0.19, p=.850. Equivalence bounds +-0.081 met (p=.017, .040). Single models: GPT-4 .15, GPT-4+Bing .16, Bard .19, Falcon .21, Claude 2 .21, Llama-2-70B .25, Coral .38. ANOVA F(12,354)=2.64, p=.002.
limits: Only 31 questions; wide equivalence bounds; best single model GPT-4 (.15) beat the ensemble median (.20). GPT-4 vs GPT-4+Bing (internet access) showed no significant difference.
agent_relevance: Cross-model ensembles add value, but a lone best model can match them. Voting helps only when errors differ (G4).

source: Schoenegger, Tuminauskaite, Park, Bastos, Tetlock (2024) Wisdom of the Silicon Crowd - acquiescence bias
finding: LLMs lean toward yes: mean ensemble forecast 57.35% while only 14 of 31 (about 45%) resolved yes. Median aggregation still gave parity with humans.
numbers: Mean forecast M=57.35 (SD 20.93), t(1006)=86.20 vs 50. 14 of 31 resolved positive.
limits: One question set; Bench to the Future later sees the same yes lean, partly from a No-heavy base rate.
agent_relevance: Add a base-rate check; do not let narrative evidence pull probabilities upward.

source: Schoenegger, Tuminauskaite, Park, Bastos, Tetlock (2024) Wisdom of the Silicon Crowd - Study 2 (crowd adjustment)
finding: Showing the human crowd median to GPT-4 and Claude 2 and letting them revise improved accuracy.
numbers: 186 primary and 186 updated forecasts. GPT-4 Brier .17 (SD .13) to .14 (SD .11), p=.003. Claude 2 .22 (SD .19) to .15 (SD .14), p<.001. Abstract: improvement 17% to 28%. Claude 2 interval width 11.67 to 8.28 after exposure.
limits: Same 31 questions; models were told the crowd median, so the benefit needs a good external prior.
agent_relevance: A strong external anchor gives .03-.07 Brier for weak models, far more than the .003 in Halawi (a stronger model). Anchoring helps weak forecasters most.

source: Karger et al. (2025) ForecastBench - news retrieval and crowd values
finding: Seven LLM baselines on 1,000 questions, including news retrieval and 'freeze values' (market crowd price at question time). Access to recent topical news did NOT improve performance. Best LLMs used the crowd price.
numbers: 200-question subset: superforecasters .096, public median .121, best LLM Claude-3.5-Sonnet freeze values + scratchpad .128 (p<.001 vs superforecasters), same with news .132. Full 1,000: Gemini-1.5-Pro freeze values scratchpad .123 (best), GPT-4o .126, Gemini with news + freeze .128.
quote: Access to recent topical news related to the questions did not improve performance.
limits: News rows are 0.004-0.005 worse than matching no-news rows, but intervals overlap. Retrieval pipeline is the Halawi one.
agent_relevance: News retrieval is not a free win; value depends on freshness and filtering. Search must be targeted and gated.

source: Karger et al. (2025) ForecastBench - LLM ensemble baseline
finding: LLM ensemble baseline: 3 models (GPT-4o, Claude-3.5-Sonnet, Gemini-1.5-Pro) x 3 superforecaster-written prompts = 9 forecasts per question, aggregated.
numbers: Candidate Brier on Halawi data (scratchpad): Claude-3.5-Sonnet .178, GPT-4o .207, Gemini-1.5-Pro .214, Qwen-1.5-110B .222, Llama-3-70B .232, Mistral-Large .233. Correlation between Arena score and Brier r=-0.68 (p=.003).
limits: Models were selected on the Halawi data (mild selection effect). I did not capture the ensemble row Brier from the results table.
agent_relevance: Mixed models x mixed prompts is the common recipe. Note G4: persona prompts are not a proven source of independence on single-answer problems.

source: Schoenegger, Park, Karger, Trott, Tetlock (2024) AI-Augmented Predictions: LLM Assistants Improve Human Forecasting Accuracy
finding: Preregistered RCT: humans who could consult a frontier LLM assistant forecast better, even with an overconfident, base-rate-neglecting assistant.
numbers: N=991, 6 questions. Accuracy up 24% to 28% vs control. Excluding one outlier question: superforecasting assistant +41%, noisy assistant +29%.
limits: Humans, not an agent; one outlier item drives the main figure; effects on crowd diversity not consistent.
agent_relevance: An imperfect advisor still helps if the integrator weighs it; for an agent, external input works as a prior, not as truth.

source: Turtel, Franklin, Skotheim, Hewitt, Schoenegger (2025) Outcome-based Reinforcement Learning to Predict the Future (TMLR)
finding: A 14B model trained with RL on Polymarket outcomes, using Exa.ai news headlines and a 7-run ensemble, beat OpenAI o1 on Brier and calibration but not the market.
numbers: 1,265-question hold-out. Soft Brier: ReMax Ensemble-7 .190 [.178,.203], ECE .062; Modified-GRPO .192; o1 .202, ECE .093; DeepSeek-R1 14B base .215, ECE .089; market is .039 better than the ensemble (p<.001). Single ReMax 10k-trained .199 [.187,.211]. Simulated bets $52 vs $39 for o1.
limits: Ensemble gain is confounded with 10x more training data (.199 to .190). Still behind the market.
agent_relevance: Seven samples plus more data gave about .009. RL on outcomes is a separate subfield; note only the ensemble size of 7.

source: Wildman et al. (FutureSearch) (2025) Bench to the Future - run-to-run noise
finding: Single LLM forecasts are noisy; averaging 5 runs cuts the standard deviation by about two thirds. Single runs sometimes swing from under 20% to over 80% on the same question.
numbers: 20 repeat forecasts on 18 questions, Gemini 2.5 Pro. Mean of 5 (bootstrapped) cut SD by about 2/3 for every approach. Variable-evidence forecaster SD about 1.7x fixed-evidence: about 60% of variance from the final judgment prompt, 40% from gathering. Fixed-evidence SD was higher than no-evidence.
limits: 18 questions, one model; 60/40 split approximate.
agent_relevance: Direct evidence for S3: averaging cuts variance, and most variance sits in the judgment step, so average the judgment, not only search. Longer context raised noise.

source: Wildman et al. (FutureSearch) (2025) Bench to the Future - agentic search and pastcasting
finding: Agentic ReAct search beat a fixed breadth-first evidence pipeline for every model; authors read it as depth over breadth. 299 questions, about 20,000 scraped pages per question (RetroSearch). No-evidence forecasters still beat the 50% line.
numbers: Brier (paired t-tests, no multiple-test correction): Sonnet 3.5 original .1925, 3.5 v2 .1690, 3.7 thinking .1645, Sonnet 4 .1560 (p=.0024 vs original), Gemini 2.5 Pro .1611. No significant gain from thinking models. Live vs retro: good distribution agreement on 20 separate questions, some higher variance in retro.
limits: Newer models also know more recent facts (confound). Most pairwise comparisons not significant.
agent_relevance: Prefer iterative targeted search over a fixed wide sweep; supports search only on a signal (G1).

source: Lu (2025) Evaluating LLMs on Real-World Forecasting Against Expert Forecasters
finding: Frontier reasoning models with AskNews summaries scored better than the published Metaculus crowd Brier but are claimed to trail experts. Five draws per question averaged; mean and median nearly identical.
numbers: 464 Metaculus questions, 5 draws, AskNews 30 summarised articles. Brier median/mean ensemble: o3 .1352/.1362, o3-pro .1386/.1389, GPT-4.1 .1542/.1509, o4-mini .1589/.1589, DeepSeek-v3 .1798/.1761, GPT-4o .1883/.1851, DeepSeek-R1 .1950/.1914, GPT-4o-mini .2743/.2676. Crowd .149 (Halawi's set). Narrative prompt worse. Experts: mean Brier .1573, median .0225 on 157 questions.
limits: Cross-set comparison to .149 is invalid. The expert mean (.1573) is worse than o3 (.1352), which conflicts with the abstract; the paper is inconsistent. AskNews beat Perplexity because fresher; Perplexity sometimes returned years-old articles.
agent_relevance: Mean vs median across 5 draws differ by under .004: aggregation rule matters little. Freshness of retrieval matters more than provider.

source: Pratt, Blumberg, Carolino, Morency (2024) Can Language Models Use Forecasting Strategies?
finding: Failed replication of retrieval helping: on a Glean dataset a single basic prompt beat every elaborate strategy, including a News API strategy (NYT and Hacker News headlines), and even the human prediction-market baseline.
numbers: Validation Brier: human .1334, basic .1221, News API .1235 (best strategy, still worse than basic), others .1483, .1895, .1562, .1553, .1706. Class-balanced weighted Brier: human .1746 beats all LLMs (basic .1955, News API .1950). Models guess low probabilities.
limits: Headline-only news sources; unbalanced outcomes; weighted Brier reverses the human-vs-LLM ranking. Older model.
agent_relevance: Boundary condition: weak retrieval adds nothing; an apparent win of a basic prompt can be a base-rate artefact. Report class-balanced scores.

source: Paleka, Goel, Fraenken, Tramer et al. (2025) Pitfalls in Evaluating Language Model Forecasters
finding: Two pitfalls for retrieval-augmented forecasters: date-restricted search leaks future information, and backtests leak logically. Claims that LLMs 'match human performance' may be circular.
numbers: Examples: search 'jan 6' limited to before 2020 returns a top hit about US politics; 'wuhan' before Dec 2018 returns Institute of Virology pages. Page date metadata often wrong; rankers trained on future data.
limits: Qualitative examples; no overall leakage rate.
agent_relevance: Any retrieval evaluation for our agent must check freshness and leakage; date filters cannot be trusted.

source: Paleka et al. (2025) Consistency Checks for Language Model Forecasters
finding: Instant, arbitrage-based consistency metrics correlate with later Brier scores of LLM forecasters. Gives a way to check forecasts without waiting for outcomes.
numbers: Aggregate arbitrage and frequentist violation scores correlate strongly with average Brier on a scraped question set and a NewsAPI set (Figure 3, values not transcribed).
limits: Correlation values are in figures I did not transcribe; no direct ensembling experiment.
agent_relevance: A code-run consistency check (P(A)+P(not A)=1 etc.) is a cheap disagreement signal for G1 and supports G5 coherence.

source: Zhang, Stadie (2026) One Fabrication Is Enough: A Fake News Article Changes the Forecasts of LLM Forecasting Systems
finding: One fabricated news article in context reverses 74-82% of forecasts that opposed it, on every frontier model tested. Retrieval-heavy forecasting architectures retrieve the fake in about 90% of runs.
numbers: Abstract: reversal 74% to 82%; two deployed architectures retrieve the fabricated article in about 90% of runs; a placebo article in the same position changes the forecast one third as often. Passage filtering discards 39% of genuine news. Single-retrieval reference system reaches the article in 17-33% of runs.
limits: Stock and prediction-market questions. Accuracy barely changes on average because the attacker's direction is right about half the time, so accuracy cannot reveal the harm.
agent_relevance: Retrieval is the attack surface. Treat single-source claims as weak (G2) and require independent corroboration.

source: Lu, Zhang (2026) The Corroboration Illusion: When More News Makes LLM Forecasts Less True
finding: Retrieval hurt small 7-8B forecasters on 500 ForecastBench questions: Brier rose from .159 (no retrieval) to .250 (RAG), with an optimism bias that grows with the number of retrieved documents. A calibrated prompt recovered to .184.
numbers: Qwen-vanilla no retrieval .159 (AUC .707), RAG .250 (AUC .722); Qwen-calibrated RAG .184 (AUC .744); Hermes no retrieval .192, RAG .226 (AUC .750). Mean forecast 0.20 with no documents vs 0.46 with 3-5. Constant base rate (.15) gives .127; market price .074.
limits: Only 7-8B open models; frontier models may be less affected. Corpus 17.4M Common Crawl News with strict crawl-date cutoff. Discrimination (AUC) improved while calibration got worse.
agent_relevance: Strong boundary condition: retrieval raises ranking ability but can wreck calibration. A constant base rate beat every no-calibration forecaster, so always compare to the base rate (G7).

source: Lu, Zhang (2026) Corroboration Illusion - poisoning and defenses
finding: One injected article per question flips 56% of forecasts, five flip 69-73%, Brier .18 to .37. Three cheap defenses each have a bypass. Isolate-then-aggregate (forecast per article, then combine) halves the effect but does not remove it.
numbers: Allow-list: unknown publisher effect -0.004 (14% flip) but spoofed publisher +0.213 (77%). Isolate-aggregate: k=1 +0.028 (18%), k=5 +0.132 (52%), clean Brier .222 vs .250. Perplexity filter: temperature 1.2 text evades (+0.174, 67%). Injected articles retrieved for 84% of pairs, mean relevance 5.8 vs 3.4 organic.
limits: Synthetic LLM-written attack; small forecaster models.
agent_relevance: Per-source independent forecasts combined in code (an ensemble over evidence) is the most robust of the three; supports G5.

source: Metaculus (2025) Q1 2025 AI Benchmark results (notebook; via page summary)
finding: Bots lost to pros head-to-head. Top bots ensembled several runs; search provider differences not significant; base model mattered more than scaffold.
numbers: Bot team vs pro team Q1 2025: -17.7 (95% CI -28.3 to -7.0), 96 questions, p=.001. Q3 2024 -11.3, Q4 2024 -8.9. Community-prediction cup team beat the bot team by 4.8 on 27 questions. 617 participants, 42 questions: Community Prediction 3rd, metac-o1 25th, metac-gpt-4o 547th. metac-o1 forecast 5 times and aggregated; 10 prize winners used median or mean; AskNews bots beat Exa and Perplexity, not significant; twsummerbot (gpt-4o only) 8th with 50-100 calls per question.
limits: Read through a page-fetch summariser, not raw HTML; p-values inconsistent in the page (.0007 vs .001); no xAI or Cassi information found.
agent_relevance: Ensembling is normal and modest; the strongest lever is the base model. 50-100 calls on a weak model reached the top 10.

source: Metaculus FutureEval spring 2026 results (via LessWrong; page summary)
finding: By spring 2026 the bot team nearly closed the gap to pros, and adding more bots to the team did not help beyond about 2-10.
numbers: 10 pros beat the top-10 bot team by 1.25 points (one-sided p=.247, not significant) vs 20.03 in Q2 2025. Top bot GreeneiBot2; best open source nostreambot, 11th. Team of 2-10 about -2 vs top bot alone -4.51; decline beyond 10, plateau near 50. No search provider clearly better. Higher-reasoning twin beat the standard twin in 8 of 8 pairs (p=.004). Bots +3.47 numeric, -2.51 binary, -5.02 multiple choice. A bot named cassi ranked 6th in team selection (only mention of Cassi found; no xAI detail).
limits: Secondary source via a summariser; hobbyists were 7 of the top 10 bot makers.
agent_relevance: Ensemble of 2-10 is the sweet spot; beyond that correlated errors give no gain (G4). Reasoning effort mattered more than search brand.

source: Synthesis of 11 analyses, 'AI forecasting in 2026' (LessWrong; page summary)
finding: Fall 2025 bot-maker survey: ensembling and multi-source research are the norm; winners made more calls and used more research sources.
numbers: 86% of Fall 2025 winners ensemble or aggregate. Winners averaged about 28 LLM calls vs 7 for non-winners (p=.022). Research providers vs score r=0.42; winners 1.75 sources vs 1.00. Removing search degraded Brier 3.6x (AIA Forecaster live eval). 34% of winners looked up similar resolved questions vs 0% of non-winners (Fisher p=.04). Platt scaling improved bot Brier by .016 binary and .005 multiple choice. Prompt tuned to match the community prediction scored +2.76 vs +4.71 for its baseline over 351-354 questions. Mantic ensemble uses Grok 4, Gemini 3 Pro, GPT-5, fine-tuned gpt-oss-120b.
limits: Secondary source via a summariser; survey is observational and self-reported; small n.
agent_relevance: Multiple sources and look-ups of similar resolved questions (analogy to base rates) correlate with winning. Platt calibration is worth .005-.016.

source: Diversity is the Strength of the AI Crowd (2026; Metaculus AI Benchmark Q2 2025 binary subset; via page summary)
finding: Cross-model ensembles beat repeated sampling of one model; the best allocation of a 5-call budget was never one model alone.
numbers: N=113 binary questions; Gemini 3 Pro, GPT-5, Grok 4, Kimi K2.5, RL fine-tuned gpt-oss-120b; R=3 samples each. Optimal 5-call allocation: FT 2, Gemini 1, GPT-5 1, Grok 4 1. Replaceability: Grok 4 about 1.7 bp, FT 0.6 bp, GPT-5 and Gemini under 0.1 bp. Weighted arithmetic mean clipped to .05 of 0 or 1. Metaculus baseline score, not Brier.
limits: No bootstrap CIs; one tournament; fixed aggregator; 3-sample cap; read via summariser.
agent_relevance: Direct support for G4: models that differ (Grok 4, fine-tuned) add more than another GPT-5 or Gemini sample. Choose ensemble members for low correlation, not only score.

source: Cross-check of the human-crowd benchmark across LLM forecasting papers
finding: Human-crowd Brier differs by question set, so papers cannot be compared directly.
numbers: Halawi crowd .149 (test); Schoenegger human crowd .19 (31 questions); ForecastBench public .121 and superforecasters .096 (200 questions); Lu cites o3 .1352 against .149.
limits: Brier is not comparable across question sets.
agent_relevance: Compare only inside one set: our agent needs a plain-model control on the same questions (G7).
